blocks.text: The honest answer to "where do I park at Bondi?" is this: yes, there's free, unrestricted parking, but it's in the residential streets north of Blair Street — about a 5–7 minute walk from the sand — and on a sunny weekend you need to be in it before roughly 9am. Everything closer is paid or time-limited. Here's every option, and what each one is actually good for.

items.label: Closest paid
items.value: Queen Elizabeth Drive car park (~500 bays)

blocks.text: The free streets north of Blair Street

My go-to on a busy day is the residential grid north of Blair Street — the streets climbing away from the water: Warners Avenue, Brassie Street, Niblick Street, Patterson Street, Oakley Road, O'Donnell Street, the top of Gould Street, Knowles Avenue, Frederick Street, Wairoa Avenue and Mitchell Street. These are genuinely free and unrestricted around the clock — no meters, no time limits. A trick for getting your bearings: drop "74 Blair Street" into Google Maps and it lands you at the edge of the zone, then park in the streets just north of there (Blair Street itself isn't free — start one block north). The trade-off is the walk and the timing. On weekdays the bays hold until residents come home in the late afternoon; on a sunny weekend they fill from mid-morning, which is exactly why arriving early matters.

The closer you get to the water, the more those free bays give way to Waverley Council Resident Parking Scheme zones — a free-looking bay near the beach can quietly be permit-only. My rule is simple: keep heading north until the restriction signs drop off, then park. The blocks behind the southern end are my quiet secret too — everyone aims for the middle of the beach, so the south end often has room when the north is chaos.

Read the closest sign every single time, even if the car in front of you is parked there. Time limits, permit zones and no-stopping lines change street by street in Bondi, and inspectors patrol hard on weekends. Blocking a driveway is one of the costliest tickets you can collect — never worth it for a five-minute dash.
When I've got beach gear, kids, or it's just too hot to walk, I pay. Roughly in order of how close they sit to the sand:

items: Queen Elizabeth Drive car park — Waverley Council's own metered car park running right behind the beach, with around 500 bays. It's the closest and most convenient, and the first to fill on a nice day, so treat it as an early-morning play.

Campbell Parade meters — the paid on-street bays opposite the beach. Handy for a quick visit, but time-limited and the priciest per hour, so they suit a coffee-and-a-swim rather than a full beach day.
The Notts Avenue / Icebergs (south) end — metered street parking down toward the pool. Limited and sought-after, but a lovely spot to land if you time it right.
Side streets a block or two back — often overlooked once the beachfront meters are full; check the posted rate and time limit at the sign before you leave the car.

blocks.text: The council's beach meters are pay-by-plate — there's no paper ticket. Enter your number plate at the machine, or (far easier) pay from your phone through the PayStay app; the meters also take the NSW Park'nPay app. They run 7am to 7pm seven days a week and switch off after 7pm, so an evening swim is one of the few times the beachfront comes free. On rates I won't bake a dollar figure into this page: Waverley reviews meter prices and charges more for beach-adjacent bays in summer than for streets further back, so check the current rate on the council's parking page and budget a daily total before you go.

blocks.title: Staying all day, often?
blocks.text: A Waverley Council beach parking permit lets you park for unlimited time in the metered bays on Queen Elizabeth Drive and Park Drive without feeding the meter. Anyone can apply, but residents, ratepayers, local teachers and active Surf Life Saving members get a lower rate — if you're a Bondi regular it can pay for itself. Eligibility and fees are set by the council, so check the current terms on the beach parking permit page.
Accessible parking and the busy-day plan

There are designated accessible bays around the beachfront, including near Queen Elizabeth Drive and the Bondi Pavilion, and a valid Mobility Parking Scheme permit gives concessions on time limits in metered and timed bays. Exact bay locations and any current works can change, so confirm on the council's parking page or with the Pavilion before relying on a specific spot.

And on a perfect summer Saturday? Don't fight it. Drive to Bondi Junction, park there, and jump on the 333 — the "Bondi Link", Sydney's busiest bus route, which runs 24 hours and connects Circular Quay to North Bondi via the Junction. On a hot weekend that short ride down Bondi Road genuinely beats doing laps for a beachfront bay. Tap on with an Opal card or contactless, and check Transport for NSW for live times.

items.q: Is there free parking at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Yes — the residential streets north of Blair Street, heading away from the water, have free, unrestricted bays about a 5–7 minute walk from the sand. Watch for permit-only and timed zones closer to the beach, and get in before about 9am on sunny weekends.

items.q: What's the closest car park to Bondi Beach?
items.a: Waverley Council's Queen Elizabeth Drive car park, a metered car park of around 500 bays right behind the beach. It's the first to fill on a nice day, so arrive early or have a backup ready.

items.q: What hours do the Bondi meters run, and how do I pay?
items.a: The beachfront meters operate 7am to 7pm, seven days a week, and switch off after 7pm. They're pay-by-plate — enter your number plate at the machine, or pay from your phone using the PayStay or NSW Park'nPay app. Rates are set by the council and are higher for beach-adjacent bays in summer, so check the current figure on Waverley's parking page.

items.q: When should I arrive to actually find a spot?
items.a: Before about 9am, or after 7pm once the meters switch off, on busy weekends and holidays. The 9am–3pm window is the hardest; if you're arriving then, plan on a paid meter, the South Bondi streets, or the Bondi Junction park-and-ride.
